title: India's Antibiotic Crisis Is a Failure of Hospital Care, Not Just Overuse
excerpt: An ICMR study of 159,336 patients found most infections from four major bacteria were carbapenem-resistant, with bloodstream mortality up to 50.8% and treatment costs roughly double.
body:
• A study across 20 Indian tertiary hospitals found 61.1% of confirmed infections from four major bacteria were resistant to carbapenems, the antibiotics doctors reach for when standard drugs fail.
  • Resistant bloodstream infections killed between 39.3% and 50.8% of patients depending on the bacteria, and more than 85% of those bloodstream infections were picked up inside healthcare facilities.
  • Treating a resistant E. coli infection cost about ₹39,846 per patient in antibiotics alone, roughly double the ₹20,034 for a drug-susceptible case, using government Jan Aushadhi rates.
  • For families arranging hospital care in India: ask whether a culture test was done before antibiotics were started, and favour hospitals with an active antimicrobial stewardship programme.

India's antibiotic resistance problem is usually blamed on patients who self-medicate and chemists who sell antibiotics without prescriptions. A major study from the Indian Council of Medical Research's surveillance network points somewhere else: at the hospitals themselves. The delivery of care — slow diagnostics, weak infection control and antibiotics prescribed before any test result exists — is what turns treatable infections into fatal ones.

What the ICMR study found

Researchers analysed 159,336 hospitalised patients across 20 tertiary-care hospitals between April 2022 and April 2025. Of these, 26,213 had confirmed infections caused by four major gram-negative bacteria: E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Some 16,025 of those patients — 61.1% — had infections resistant to carbapenems, among the strongest antibiotics in routine use.

The consequences show in the mortality figures. Deaths among patients with resistant infections ran at 24.4% for E. coli, 31.2% for K. pneumoniae, 37.9% for A. baumannii and 28.9% for P. aeruginosa, each several points higher than for susceptible infections. In bloodstream infections the gap widened sharply: mortality ranged from 39.3% to 50.8%. More than 85% of those bloodstream infections were healthcare-associated, meaning patients acquired them during treatment rather than bringing them in from the community.

Slower, costlier, harder to treat

Resistance also doubles the bill. Antibiotic costs for resistant infections ran 1.1 to two times higher than for susceptible ones; for E. coli, the figure was about ₹39,846 per patient against ₹20,034. Those numbers use national Jan Aushadhi generic rates, so private-hospital bills are likely higher. A separate narrative review from AIIMS Bhopal researchers, published in Frontiers in Antibiotics, put the mortality rate for multidrug-resistant infections at 13.1% and found median treatment costs of US$199 per case against US$109 for susceptible infections.

The review also documented how uneven the threat is. MRSA prevalence in Bihar reached 65%, well above the reported national average of 47.8%, and outpatient E. coli isolates in surveillance data nearly tripled between 2018 and 2023 — a sign that resistance is now entrenched outside hospitals too.

Why the fix is systemic

Clinicians describe the same chain of failures: a patient arrives with a serious infection, laboratory culture results take days, so doctors prescribe broad-spectrum antibiotics empirically and hope. Hospitals with crowded wards and thin infection-control staffing then spread resistant organisms between patients. An India Today analysis framed the remedy in three parts — safer hospitals, faster diagnostics and cleaner medicines — arguing that prescribing behaviour cannot change until the system around the prescriber does.

What this means for diaspora families

NRIs routinely make medical decisions for parents in India, and increasingly travel there for planned procedures. The practical checks are simple: confirm the hospital runs culture tests before or alongside the first antibiotic dose, ask whether it publishes infection-rate data, and treat a long antibiotic course without a named organism as a question worth asking, not a detail to accept. India's resistance rates are now high enough that these questions belong in every hospital admission conversation.
